title: kv-cache-management-investigation-2026-04-02
content:
Purpose:
This is a working investigation into KV cache management trade-offs: reuse rates, eviction policies, paging behavior, and memory-bandwidth impact. The goal is to identify a set of practical defaults and targeted optimizations to reduce token cost and tail latency for long-context batched workloads on our A100/H100 clusters.

Background/Context:
- We observed increased p99 latencies and token cost for workloads with long historical context (3k-32k tokens) when KV cache reuse is low or when eviction triggers paging to host memory.
- Existing experiments (see linked artifacts) focused on pure reuse and LRU eviction; this doc expands to measure memory bandwidth implications and paging penalties across model sizes.

Testbed:
- HW: NVIDIA A100 80GB, NVIDIA H100 80GB (mixed results noted), PCIe gen4 interconnect, NVMe swap on local SSD for paging tests.
- SW: serving-runtime @ main (commit 9f2a3b), kernel selection disabled for controlled comparison, quantized FP16/native kernels where applicable.
- Models: rw-llama-13b-v2 (dense), rw-llama-30b-8bit.
- Workloads: synthetic chat traces derived from production traces with sequence length distributions: short(<=512), medium(512-2048), long(2048-32768).
- Metrics: throughput (tokens/s), latency P50/P95/P99 (ms per request), KV reuse rate (fraction of tokens whose KV state is reused vs re-generated), memory bandwidth (GB/s measured via nvprof/NSYS counters), swap/paging incidence and latency penalty.

Experiment matrix:
1) Eviction policy: LRU vs Segmented LRU (probation/keep) vs Random
2) KV cache size: 4GB, 8GB, 16GB allocated per model instance
3) Batching: micro-batch sizes 1, 4, 16 (to model PLG burstiness)
4) Paging behavior: disabled (OOM), enabled->swap to host memory (NVMe), soft-eviction threshold at 90% vs 75%
5) Model size: 13B vs 30B

Key findings (summary):
- Reuse rate is the dominant factor for token cost: increasing reuse from 40% -> 70% lowered per-token compute by ~32% on average.
- Eviction policy matters most under constrained cache sizes and long contexts. Segmented LRU (SLRU) improved reuse by 6-12% over plain LRU for heavy-tail access patterns we saw in chat traces.
- Paging to host memory is catastrophic for p99: when paging occurred, p99 latency increased 3.5x-6x depending on NVMe performance; throughput dropped by 40-70%.
- Memory bandwidth observed on A100: KV access + kernel memory copies peaked at ~380 GB/s combined when many concurrent streams hit the KV area; H100 numbers were similar but showed higher variance.
- When KV cache is sized to hold the working set for the top 80% of requests (by reuse distribution), we hit a sweet spot: modest memory cost for significant latency improvement.

Representative numbers (rw-llama-13b, medium/long mix):
- Baseline (LRU, 8GB KV, batch=4, reuse=45%): throughput 22k tokens/s, p50 18ms, p95 85ms, p99 240ms, mem bw 290 GB/s
- SLRU (8GB, batch=4, reuse=53%): throughput 28.2k tokens/s (+28%), p50 16ms, p95 62ms, p99 160ms, mem bw 310 GB/s
- LRU (4GB, batch=4, reuse=32%): throughput 15.7k tokens/s, p99 420ms (paging events observed), paging penalty per event ~110ms
- LRU (8GB but paging enabled with soft threshold 75%): p99 520ms when NVMe stressed, throughput 12k tokens/s (-46%)

Memory-bandwidth analysis notes:
- On A100, concurrent KV reads from multiple streams saturate HBM channels; when we add kernel execution overhead, the combined effective BW is ~340-390 GB/s. This correlates with increased stalls when KV is fragmented and accesses are non-coalesced.
- Paging increases PCIe/NVMe IO; measured NVMe read bw peaks at ~7 GB/s (local NVMe), which is orders of magnitude lower than HBM, explaining the p99 explosion.
- Observed that SLAB-style allocation for KV blocks improves coalescing and reduces HBM pressure by ~8% in microbenchmarks.

Eviction policy deep-dive:
- LRU: simple, decent steady-state, but thrashes on workloads with temporal locality shifts (e.g., many short chats interleaved with a few long sessions).
- SLRU: keeps a probation bucket that filters hot items into a protected segment; cut down churn for long interactions that return to previous context. Net effect: higher reuse and fewer refills.
- LFU-like policies: in our tests, pure LFU suffered from cold-start inertia and was worse for bursty chat workloads. A hybrid (LFU with decay) might help but we didn't fully explore yet.

Paging and remote spill strategy:
- Spilling to host memory (DRAM) would be marginally better than NVMe but still slower than HBM; our on-host DRAM is only accessible via PCIe and shows 20-40x slower latency for the KV miss path.
- NVMe spill is too costly for p99-sensitive routes. For background/throughput-oriented routes, a configurable spill-to-disk with aggressive prefetch could be acceptable.
- Recommendation: Disable automatic paging for latency-sensitive endpoints. Prefer eviction (SLRU) + admission heuristics. Provide a spill mode only for best-effort routes.

Actionable recommendations:
1) Default eviction: switch to SLRU with two segments (probation=25%, protected=75%) and tune probation promotion threshold based on observed inter-request intervals.
2) Cache sizing heuristic: autosize KV to hold top 80% of working set by sampling reuse distribution over a 24h window. Expose a customer knob to bump this to 90% for latency-critical customers.
3) Paging policy: default to disabled for hosted/enterprise low-p99 tiers. Add explicit service tier flag to enable spill for batch/low-priority routes.
4) Allocation: adopt slab allocation to reduce fragmentation and improve HBM coalescing.
5) Instrumentation: add counters for eviction churn, paging events, and per-request KV read bytes. Surface these in Redwood Console under per-route debugging.
6) Short-term perf fixes: micro-op fusion in kernel for KV prefetch and reduce memcpy copies between KV area and compute tensors.

Open questions / next experiments:
- Quantify tradeoffs for SLRU parameters (probation size, promotion threshold) on real production traces across regions.
- Evaluate hybrid LFU-decay policy with time-based decay on medium-length sessions.
- Test host DRAM spill (NUMA-aware) vs NVMe on H100 interconnects - measure practical p99 deltas.
- Explore prefetching strategies: predictive prefetch for likely continuation tokens using a lightweight n-gram model.

Immediate next steps (owners):
- Priya: implement SLRU prototype in runtime, expose probation size flag (ETA 2 weeks).
- Miguel: add per-request KV metrics and dashboard prototype in Console (ETA 1 week).
- Jordan: run 48h sampling job on production traces to produce reuse distribution histograms and working set sizes (ETA 3 days).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working doc; numbers are from controlled lab runs and should be validated on carrots-prod traces before making global defaults.
- If we adopt SLRU by default, we should stage rollout using canary routing (10% traffic) with rollback triggers on cost or p99 regressions.

Appendix: raw microbenchmark snippet (repro instructions)
- branch: feature/kv-slru-experiment (see linked GH PR)
- run script: tools/bench/kv_working_set.sh --model rw-llama-13b --batch 4 --seq-dist long --kv-size 8GB --eviction slru
- collect: nsys profile + runtime counters, upload to s3://redwood-bench/kv-slru/2026-03-30

End of note.
